blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 14 (Simple Harmonic Motion), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is oscillatory motion? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: Oscillatory motion is a to and fro motion about a mean position; it is periodic and repeats itself after equal intervals of time. Examples: a vibrating tuning fork; a mass oscillating at the end of a spring.

book_ref.quote: Oscillatory motion is a to and fro motion about its mean position

blocks.prompt: 2 What causes a displaced body to oscillate about its mean position?
blocks.explanation: When the body is displaced from its mean (equilibrium) position, a restoring force acts on it and brings it back to the equilibrium position. This restoring force causes the oscillation of the body.

book_ref.quote: All the bodies that undergo vibrational or oscillation motion have an equilibrium position or mean position

blocks.prompt: 3 Name four natural phenomena that show periodic motion.
blocks.explanation: Motion of the Earth around the Sun, motion of the Moon around the Earth, water waves and sound waves (also a tuning fork and a rocking chair).

book_ref.quote: Many natural phenomena show periodic motion.

blocks.prompt: 4 Define vibration. What is one vibration of a simple pendulum swinging between A and B?
blocks.explanation: One complete round trip (cycle) of a vibrating body about its mean position is called a vibration. For the pendulum, motion of the bob from A to B and back from B to A, crossing the mean position, is one vibration.

book_ref.quote: One complete round trip (cycle) of vibrating body about its mean position is called vibration

blocks.prompt: 5 Differentiate between instantaneous displacement and amplitude.
blocks.explanation: Displacement changes from instant to instant; amplitude is its fixed maximum value.

book_ref.quote: The magnitude of the maximum displacement of the vibrating body on either side of its mean position

rows: Distance of the vibrating body from the mean position at any instant.
Magnitude of the maximum displacement on either side of the mean position.
Changes continuously during the motion (zero at the mean position).
Constant for a given oscillation (if there is no damping).
For the pendulum: OA = OB = x₀.

blocks.prompt: 6 How is the amplitude of a wave related to the energy it carries?
blocks.explanation: Amplitude measures the energy carried by a wave: the greater the amplitude of the wave, the greater the energy carried by it, and vice versa.

book_ref.quote: Amplitude of a wave measures the energy carried by a wave.

blocks.prompt: 7 A pendulum has amplitude 5 cm. What distance does the bob cover in 3 complete vibrations?
blocks.explanation: In one vibration the bob goes from the mean position to one extreme, back, to the other extreme and back: distance = 4x₀ = 4 × 5 cm = 20 cm. In 3 vibrations: 3 × 20 cm = 60 cm.

book_ref.quote: If x₀ is the amplitude of simple pendulum

blocks.prompt: 8 Define frequency and its SI unit. Give its dimension.
blocks.explanation: Frequency is the number of vibrations completed by a vibrating body in one second: f = n/t = 1/T. Its unit is the hertz (Hz); one hertz is one oscillation per second. Dimension: [T⁻¹].

book_ref.quote: Frequency is defined as the number of vibrations or oscillations (n) completed by the vibrating body in one second

blocks.prompt: 9 A mass on a spring makes 30 vibrations in 12 s. Find its time period and frequency.

book_ref.quote: A fish connected to a spring makes 10 vibrations in 20 seconds

blocks.prompt: 10 Define angular frequency and show that ω = 2πf.
blocks.explanation: Angular frequency is the angular displacement per unit time: ω = θ/t. For one revolution θ = 2π rad and t = T, so ω = 2π/T. Since f = 1/T, ω = 2πf. Unit: rad s⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: Angular displacement per unit time is called angular frequency

blocks.prompt: 11 Differentiate between frequency and angular frequency.
blocks.explanation: Both have dimension [T⁻¹]; ω = 2πf.

book_ref.quote: The SI unit of angular frequency is rad s⁻¹ and its dimension is [T⁻¹].

rows: Number of vibrations completed in one second.

blocks.prompt: 12 A particle in S.H.M has angular frequency 6 rad s⁻¹. Find its frequency and time period.

book_ref.quote: A particle executing simple harmonic motion has an angular frequency of 2 rad s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 13 Write the mathematical form of S.H.M and explain the meaning of its negative sign.
blocks.explanation: a ∝ −x (a = −ω²x): the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position. The negative sign shows that the acceleration is always opposite to the displacement, i.e. directed towards the mean position.

book_ref.quote: Simple harmonic motion is a type of oscillation or vibratory motion produced under the action of restoring force.

blocks.prompt: 14 Are all periodic vibrations simple harmonic? Give an example.
blocks.explanation: No. Any restoring force can cause oscillation, but S.H.M needs a restoring force proportional to displacement. The needle of an electrocardiogram traces a periodic pattern, but its restoring force is not always proportional to displacement, so it is not S.H.M.

book_ref.quote: not all periodic vibrations are examples of simple harmonic motion

blocks.prompt: 15 What is the role of inertia in simple harmonic motion?
blocks.explanation: The restoring force depends only on displacement (F = −kx), not on inertia. Inertia is still needed: it carries the body past the mean position, where the force is zero, so the body keeps oscillating.

book_ref.quote: The restoring force is not proportional to the inertia (mass) of the body

blocks.prompt: 16 State Hooke's law for a spring. Why is the restoring force written as F = −kx?
blocks.explanation: Hooke's law: the applied force is proportional to the displacement, F = kx. The spring exerts an elastic restoring force equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the applied force, so F = −kx.

book_ref.quote: According to Hooke's law, the applied force is proportional to displacement

blocks.prompt: 17 What is the spring constant? On what does it depend? Give its SI unit.
blocks.explanation: From F = kx, the spring constant k = F/x is the force per unit extension. It depends on the nature of the spring (its material, physical shape and structure). SI unit: N m⁻¹.

book_ref.quote: where 'k' is spring constant depending upon the nature (physical shape and structure of a spring)

blocks.prompt: 18 A spring of constant 250 N m⁻¹ is compressed by 3 cm. Find the restoring force and its direction.
blocks.explanation: F = −kx = −250 × (−0.03) = +7.5 N. Magnitude 7.5 N; it acts opposite to the compression, i.e. towards the mean position.

book_ref.quote: The spring will exert the force on the body due to elastic restoring force

blocks.prompt: 19 Show that a mass attached to a horizontal spring has a ∝ −x.
blocks.explanation: Restoring force F = −kx and, by Newton's second law, F = ma. So ma = −kx, a = −(k/m)x. As k/m is constant, a ∝ −x, the mathematical form of S.H.M.

book_ref.quote: The negative sign shows that acceleration and displacement are always in opposite direction

blocks.prompt: 20 Why does a mass on a spring not stop at the mean position when released?
blocks.explanation: At the mean position the restoring force is zero, but the mass has its maximum velocity there. Due to inertia it crosses O, compresses the spring to B, and returns, so it keeps oscillating between A and B.

book_ref.quote: it will move towards 'O' and will cross the mean position O due to inertia

blocks.prompt: 21 Write the time period of a mass-spring system. How does it change with mass and with spring constant?
blocks.explanation: T = 2π√(m/k). A heavier mass gives a longer period (T ∝ √m); a stiffer spring (larger k) gives a shorter period (T ∝ 1/√k).

book_ref.quote: T is the reciprocal of f = (1/2π)√(k/m), so m/k comes under the root

blocks.prompt: 22 A 0.2 kg mass oscillates on a spring of constant 80 N m⁻¹. Find ω, f and T.

book_ref.quote: The last line should read T = 1/f = 2π√(m/k)

blocks.prompt: 23 Name three real-world applications that use the principle of S.H.M.
blocks.explanation: Pendulum clocks, musical instruments and the suspension system of vehicles.

book_ref.quote: Real world applications that utilize S.H.M principle include

blocks.prompt: 24 What is a simple pendulum?
blocks.explanation: A simple pendulum consists of a small heavy solid bob of mass m suspended from a rigid support by a light inextensible string of a certain length. When displaced and released, it oscillates about its mean position under gravity.

book_ref.quote: A simple pendulum consists of a small heavy solid bob of mass m suspended from a rigid support

blocks.prompt: 25 Which force provides the restoring force for a simple pendulum, and what happens to the other component of weight?
blocks.explanation: The weight mg is resolved at angle θ. mg sinθ, along the path towards the mean position, is the restoring force (F = −mg sinθ). mg cosθ acts along the string and is cancelled by the tension T, since there is no motion along the string.

book_ref.quote: As the pendulum has no motion along the direction of the string

blocks.prompt: 26 Why must the angle of a simple pendulum be small for its motion to be S.H.M?
blocks.explanation: The restoring acceleration is a = −g sinθ, which is not proportional to displacement in general. Only for small angles (about 10° or less) is sinθ ≈ θ (in radians) and x ≈ arc S, giving a = −(g/ℓ)x, i.e. a ∝ −x.

book_ref.quote: For small angles sinθ ≈ θ (θ in radians)

blocks.prompt: 27 Use Table 14.1 to show that sinθ ≈ θ for 5°.
blocks.explanation: From the table, 5° = 0.0873 rad and sin 5° = 0.0872. The two differ by only 0.0001 (about 0.1 %), so for small angles sinθ can be replaced by θ in radians.

book_ref.quote: Table 14.1: Values of θ and sinθ for small angle

blocks.prompt: 28 On what factors does the time period of a simple pendulum depend, and on what does it not depend?
blocks.explanation: T = 2π√(ℓ/g). T is directly proportional to √ℓ and inversely proportional to √g. It is independent of the mass of the bob and of the (small) amplitude.

book_ref.quote: The time period of motion of the pendulum is independent of the mass m of the bob and amplitude.

blocks.prompt: 29 What is a second pendulum? What is its frequency?
blocks.explanation: A pendulum that completes one vibration in two seconds (T = 2 s) is a second pendulum. Its frequency f = 1/T = 1/2 = 0.5 Hz.

book_ref.quote: A pendulum that completes one vibration in two seconds

blocks.prompt: 30 Find the time period of a simple pendulum of length 0.4 m (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

book_ref.quote: The above expression shows that the time period of simple pendulum is directly proportional to the square root

blocks.prompt: 31 How can a simple pendulum be used to find g at a place?
blocks.explanation: Measure the length ℓ of the pendulum, set it vibrating with small amplitude and measure its time period T with a stopwatch. Then g = 4π²ℓ/T² (from T = 2π√(ℓ/g)).

book_ref.quote: We measure the length 'ℓ' of the pendulum and then set the pendulum into motion.

blocks.prompt: 32 A pendulum 1.0 m long has a time period of 3.0 s on a planet. Find g on that planet.

book_ref.quote: the acceleration due to gravity is calculated by using Eq. (14.10)

blocks.prompt: 33 Find the length of a pendulum whose time period is 4 s (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

book_ref.quote: Also find its frequency at a place where the value of g is taken to be 9.8 m s⁻²

blocks.prompt: 34 Would a pendulum of fixed length have the same time period on the Earth and on the Moon? Explain.
blocks.explanation: No. T = 2π√(ℓ/g), so T ∝ 1/√g. The value of g on the Moon is smaller than on the Earth, so the same pendulum has a longer time period on the Moon.

book_ref.quote: Would the time period of a simple pendulum be same on Earth and moon

blocks.prompt: 35 Differentiate between the mass-spring system and the simple pendulum as S.H.M systems.
blocks.explanation: Both obey a ∝ −x, but different forces and constants appear.

book_ref.quote: Comparing Eqs. (14.7) and (14.8), we have

rows: Restoring force is the elastic force of the spring, F = −kx.
Restoring force is mg sinθ, a component of the weight.
T is independent of the mass of the bob.

blocks.text: 14.4 Simple Harmonic Motion and Uniform Circular Motion

blocks.prompt: 36 How can the shadow of a ball on a turntable be used to show S.H.M?
blocks.explanation: A ball attached to the rim of a turntable moves in uniform circular motion when the table rotates with constant ω. A beam of light casts its shadow on a screen; the shadow moves to and fro across the screen in S.H.M, like a body on a spring.

book_ref.quote: consider a turntable of radius r with a ball attached to its rim

blocks.prompt: 37 Write the instantaneous displacement of the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion and explain the symbols.
blocks.explanation: x = x₀ cos θ = x₀ cos ωt, where x₀ is the radius of the circle (amplitude), ω the uniform angular velocity, t the time from the starting point A and θ = ωt the angle swept by the radius OP.

book_ref.quote: Equation (14.11) gives the instantaneous displacement of point Q

blocks.prompt: 38 Where is the speed of a body in S.H.M maximum and where is it zero? Give reasons.
blocks.explanation: v = ω√(x₀² − x²). At the mean position x = 0, so v = x₀ω (maximum). At the extreme positions x = ±x₀, so v = 0.

book_ref.quote: Eq. (14.13) should read v = ω√(x₀² − x²)

blocks.prompt: 39 A body in S.H.M has amplitude 0.10 m and ω = 8 rad s⁻¹. Find its speed at x = 0.08 m.

book_ref.quote: the print drops the square on the first x₀

blocks.prompt: 40 Show that the acceleration of the projection of a particle in uniform circular motion satisfies a ∝ −x.
blocks.explanation: The centripetal acceleration of P has magnitude x₀ω² towards the centre; its horizontal component is the acceleration of Q: a = −x₀ω² cosθ = −x₀ω²(x/x₀) = −ω²x. As ω is constant, a ∝ −x, so the projection executes S.H.M.

book_ref.quote: This expression is the mathematical condition of S.H.M

blocks.prompt: 41 A 0.4 kg mass on a spring of constant 16 N m⁻¹ has amplitude 0.1 m. Find its acceleration and speed at x = 0.06 m.

book_ref.quote: A 0.2 kg mass is attached to a spring with a spring constant of 10 N m⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 42 Define phase. What is the phase constant?
blocks.explanation: Phase is the angle θ = ωt (in general ωt + φ) that specifies the displacement and the direction of motion of a point in S.H.M; it shows the state of motion. The constant φ in x = x₀ cos(ωt + φ) is the phase constant (phase angle); it depends on the displacement and velocity at t = 0.

book_ref.quote: The angle θ = ωt which specifies the displacements x as well as the direction of motion

blocks.prompt: 43 Differentiate between oscillations in phase and out of phase.
blocks.explanation: The difference is in the phase difference between the two systems.

book_ref.quote: When the phase difference between two oscillating systems is 180°

rows: Both reach the same extreme together.
When one is at +x₀ the other is at −x₀.
Displacements always have the same sign.

blocks.prompt: 44 Where is the oscillating point at t = 0 when φ = 0° and when φ = 90°?
blocks.explanation: x = x₀ cos(ωt + φ). For φ = 0°, x = x₀ cos 0 = x₀: the point starts at an extreme position. For φ = 90°, x = x₀ cos 90° = 0: the point starts at the mean position.

book_ref.quote: If φ = 90°, then Eq. (14.18) becomes:

blocks.prompt: 45 For x = x₀ cos(ωt + 180°), find the displacement at t = 0 and t = T/2.
blocks.explanation: At t = 0: x = x₀ cos 180° = −x₀. At t = T/2: ωt = π, so x = x₀ cos(360°) = +x₀. The point starts at the negative extreme.

book_ref.quote: Putting t = 0, T/4, T/2, 3T/4, T ...., we obtain a graph

blocks.prompt: 46 A body oscillates as x = 0.2 cos ωt with T = 2 s. Find its phase and displacement at t = 0.25 s.

book_ref.quote: Where x is instantaneous displacement, x₀ is maximum displacement

blocks.prompt: 47 What is the phase difference between (i) velocity and displacement (ii) acceleration and displacement in S.H.M?
blocks.explanation: (i) Velocity and displacement differ in phase by π/2. (ii) Since a = −ω²x, acceleration is always opposite to displacement, so their phase difference is π.

book_ref.quote: The phase difference between velocity and displacement is π/2.

blocks.prompt: 48 Why is the acceleration of a body in S.H.M maximum at the extreme positions?
blocks.explanation: a = −ω²x, so the magnitude of acceleration is proportional to the displacement. Displacement is largest (x₀) at the extremes, so |a| = x₀ω² is maximum there; at the mean position x = 0 and a = 0.

book_ref.quote: The acceleration will be maximum (i.e., x₀ω²) at the extreme positions

blocks.prompt: 49 Write the equations of displacement, velocity and acceleration for x = x₀ cos ωt.
blocks.explanation: Displacement: x = x₀ cos ωt. Velocity: v = −x₀ω sin ωt (magnitude x₀ω sin ωt). Acceleration: a = −ω²x = −x₀ω² cos ωt.

book_ref.quote: For x = x₀ cos ωt the velocity is v = −x₀ω sin ωt, so it falls first

blocks.prompt: 50 A body moves in S.H.M with amplitude 0.05 m and frequency 4 Hz. Find its maximum speed and maximum acceleration.

book_ref.quote: The velocity of the particle is maximum (i.e., v = x₀ω) at the mean position

blocks.prompt: 51 Why is the average force ½kx₀ used to find the work done in stretching a spring?
blocks.explanation: The restoring force is not constant: it is zero at x = 0 and kx₀ at x = x₀, increasing uniformly. So the average force is (0 + kx₀)/2 = ½kx₀, and W = F_av × x₀ = ½kx₀².

book_ref.quote: Thus, average value of force from the mean position to the extreme position is:

blocks.prompt: 52 A spring of constant 150 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 6 cm. Find its P.E. and K.E. at x = 4 cm.

book_ref.quote: This work done on the mass attached to a spring is stored in terms of potential energy

blocks.prompt: 53 Differentiate between the kinetic energy and potential energy of a mass-spring oscillator.
blocks.explanation: Their sum is constant: K.E. + P.E. = ½kx₀².

book_ref.quote: When a body is executing simple harmonic motion, it possesses both potential energy as well as kinetic energy.

rows: Due to the velocity of the mass.
Due to the displacement from the mean position (elastic P.E.).

blocks.prompt: 54 Show that the total energy of a mass-spring system is independent of the displacement x.
blocks.explanation: T.E = K.E + P.E = ½k(x₀² − x²) + ½kx² = ½kx₀². The x² terms cancel, so T.E depends only on k and the amplitude x₀, not on x; it is constant and proportional to x₀².

book_ref.quote: it is proved that total energy of mass spring system is constant

blocks.prompt: 55 Express the total energy of an oscillator in terms of m, ω and x₀ and find it for m = 0.5 kg, ω = 4 rad s⁻¹, x₀ = 0.1 m.
blocks.explanation: T.E = ½kx₀² with k = mω² gives T.E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.5 × 16 × 0.01 = 0.04 J.

book_ref.quote: Eq. (14.29) should read T.E = ½mω²x₀²

blocks.prompt: 56 At what displacement is the energy of an oscillator half kinetic and half potential?
blocks.explanation: P.E. = ½ T.E: ½kx² = ½(½kx₀²), so x² = x₀²/2 and x = x₀/√2 ≈ 0.707x₀ on either side of the mean position.

book_ref.quote: The energy oscillates between K.E. and P.E., but their sum remains constant.

blocks.prompt: 57 A 0.4 kg mass on a spring of constant 90 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 0.08 m. Find its maximum speed.

book_ref.quote: At mean position x = 0, the mass gets maximum velocity

blocks.prompt: 58 What are free vibrations? Give two examples.
blocks.explanation: A body executes free vibrations when it oscillates with its natural frequency without the interference of an external force. Examples: a simple pendulum slightly displaced and released; a guitar string (also a ringing bell).

book_ref.quote: A body is said to be executing free vibrations if it oscillates with its natural frequency

blocks.prompt: 59 Why does the amplitude of an ideal free oscillation remain constant?
blocks.explanation: In free oscillations with no resistive force, no energy is lost, so the total energy stays constant. Since T.E = ½kx₀², a constant energy means a constant amplitude.

book_ref.quote: In free oscillations, the total energy of the body remains constant

blocks.prompt: 60 Give three examples of forced vibrations.
blocks.explanation: A swing struck (pushed) repeatedly; the vibrations of a factory floor caused by running heavy machinery; the sounding wooden boards of string instruments producing loud music (also a vehicle vibrating due to its engine).

book_ref.quote: Another example of forced vibration is loud music produced by sounding wooden boards

blocks.prompt: 61 What are damped oscillations? Why does a real swing finally stop?
blocks.explanation: Oscillations whose amplitude decreases in the presence of resistive (damping) forces are damped oscillations. Air resistance and friction dissipate the swing's energy, so its amplitude becomes smaller and smaller and it finally stops.

book_ref.quote: The oscillations with decreasing amplitude in the presence of various resistive forces are called damped oscillations

blocks.prompt: 62 Differentiate between free (ideal) oscillations and damped oscillations.
blocks.explanation: The difference lies in whether energy is lost to resistive forces.

book_ref.quote: In an ideal free oscillation system, we have studied that the total mechanical energy

rows: Resistive forces such as air resistance and friction act.
Amplitude decreases with time until the body stops.

blocks.prompt: 63 Differentiate between light damping and critical damping.
blocks.explanation: They differ in how quickly the body settles at equilibrium.

book_ref.quote: Light damping: It reduces gradually the energy and amplitude of vibrating body.

rows: Energy and amplitude reduce gradually; the body keeps oscillating for a while.
The object returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time.
Example: a swing in a playground.
Example: shock absorbers in a car.

blocks.prompt: 64 Why is a damping system needed in the suspension of a car?
blocks.explanation: On a bumpy, rough road the car's springs would produce excessive oscillations. Shock absorbers damp these oscillations so the passengers get a comfortable ride.

book_ref.quote: Damping system is required to ensure a comfortable ride for the passengers

blocks.prompt: 65 What are driving force and driving frequency?
blocks.explanation: A periodic external force applied to keep the amplitude of an oscillator constant is the driving force. The oscillation it produces is a forced oscillation, and its frequency is the driving frequency.

book_ref.quote: Thus, when the oscillating body is subjected to a periodic driving force

blocks.prompt: 66 Define resonance and give one example from daily life.
blocks.explanation: When the frequency of the driving force equals the natural frequency of the oscillating body, the amplitude of vibration increases very much; this is resonance. Example: pushing a swing at its natural frequency makes its amplitude grow.

book_ref.quote: This phenomenon is known as resonance.

blocks.prompt: 67 In the pendulum experiment, why do C and D stay almost at rest when P (length ℓ₁) swings?
blocks.explanation: The vibration of P reaches all pendulums through the rod, but C and D have length ℓ₂, so their natural frequency differs from that of P. There is no resonance for them; only A and B (length ℓ₁) resonate.

book_ref.quote: At the same time, the pendulums C and D whose natural frequencies are different

blocks.prompt: 68 How does a microwave oven heat food by resonance?
blocks.explanation: The oven's microwaves (about 2.45 GHz) excite the water molecules in food, which oscillate at the same frequency and collide with one another. Friction from the collisions changes their kinetic energy into heat.

book_ref.quote: Friction generated by the collisions changes the kinetic energy of the water into heat

blocks.prompt: 69 How is resonance used in tuning a radio?
blocks.explanation: Turning the knob changes the natural frequency of the receiver's electrical circuit. When it equals the transmission frequency of a station, resonance occurs and the receiver absorbs maximum energy from that station's signal, so only that station is heard.

book_ref.quote: The tuning of an analogue radio set for a certain station is also based on resonance

blocks.prompt: 70 Why can resonance be dangerous for an aeroplane wing?
blocks.explanation: The wings experience aerodynamic forces, turbulence and engine vibration. If the frequency of these forces matches the wings' natural frequency, resonance makes the amplitude very large, which may be dangerous.

book_ref.quote: When the frequencies of these forces are matching with the natural frequency of the wings

blocks.prompt: 71 Why does a guitar or violin have a hollow wooden box?
blocks.explanation: The vibrating string transfers its energy to the hollow sound box, which resonates with the string. This amplifies the sound waves, producing a louder and richer sound.

book_ref.quote: The sound box resonants, amplifying the sound waves.

blocks.prompt: 72 How is resonance used in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)?
blocks.explanation: In MRI, strong radio frequency radiations make nuclei oscillate and the nuclei absorb energy. The pattern of the energy absorbed is used to produce a computer-enhanced picture for medical diagnosis.

book_ref.quote: strong radio frequency radiations are used to cause nuclei to oscillate

blocks.prompt: 73 How does a Rubens tube show the nodes and antinodes of a standing wave?
blocks.explanation: At the resonance frequency a standing wave forms inside the gas-filled tube. Where the pressure is high, more gas escapes from the holes and the flame is tall; where it is low, the flame is low. Tall flames stand at the pressure antinodes, half a wavelength apart.

book_ref.quote: The standing wave creates points with oscillating (higher and lower) pressure within the tube.

blocks.prompt: 74 Why does sand collect along certain lines on a vibrating Chladni plate?
blocks.explanation: When the plate vibrates at a resonant frequency, nodes and antinodes form on it. The plate does not vibrate at the nodes, so the sand is shaken off the vibrating antinodes and settles at the stationary nodes, showing the standing-wave pattern.

book_ref.quote: Hence, the sand will vibrate and shift from antinode to nodes because the nodes are stationary.

blocks.prompt: 75 Differentiate between nodes and antinodes on a vibrating Chladni plate.
blocks.explanation: Nodes and antinodes form when the plate vibrates at a resonant frequency.

book_ref.quote: When the plate is vibrated at the frequency of a resonant normal mode

rows: Points where the plate does not vibrate.
Points where the plate vibrates with maximum amplitude.
Stationary, so the sand collects there.
Sand is shaken away from them.

blocks.prompt: 76 How does an acoustic levitator hold small particles in air?
blocks.explanation: High-frequency (ultrasonic) sound from a transducer is reflected by a reflector; incident and reflected waves form a standing wave. The pressure difference between nodes (minimum) and antinodes (maximum) pushes small particles against gravity and traps them at the nodes.

book_ref.quote: The interaction between the incident and reflected waves forms a standing wave

blocks.prompt: 77 How does damping affect the amplitude and sharpness of resonance?
blocks.explanation: Both depend on damping: the smaller the damping, the greater the resonant amplitude and the sharper the resonance. A heavily damped system has a fairly flat resonance (amplitude-frequency) curve.

book_ref.quote: The amplitude as well as its sharpness, both depend upon the damping.

blocks.prompt: 78 Why does a lead bob show a much larger resonant amplitude than a pith ball of equal size on the same length?
blocks.explanation: Both are driven by a third pendulum of equal length, so both resonate. But air resistance damps the light pith ball much more than the heavy lead bob, and smaller damping gives a larger resonant amplitude.

book_ref.quote: It is observed that amplitude of the lead bob is much greater than that of the pith-ball.

blocks.prompt: 79 What happened to the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in 1940, and what lesson does it teach?
blocks.explanation: About four months after opening, a mild wind set the bridge into resonant vibrations; within a few hours the amplitude became so large that a part broke off. It shows that resonance must be considered in designing bridges and other civil engineering projects.

book_ref.quote: Only four months after this, a mild wind set up the bridge in resonant vibrations.
